newsitem.title: USA: Clinton promises help for flood-ravaged region.
newsitem.headline: Clinton promises help for flood-ravaged region.

text.p: The swollen Red River threatened to rise even higher on Tuesday as President Bill Clinton pledged to seek an additional $200 million in disaster aid for flood-ravaged region, saying he had never seen anything like it.
Clinton, who went on an inspection tour of the area, also promised that the federal government would pick up the tab for all of the immediate emergency work.

"I don't recall ever in my life seeing anything like this and I have been very impressed by the courage and the faith that all of you have shown," Clinton told officials and residents. It was, he said, "not an ordinary disaster."
Clinton flew by helicopter over Grand Forks and East Grand Forks, Minnesota, towns once separated by the Red River but now in the middle of it.
He also saw the charred aftermath of a fire that broke out on Saturday in downtown Grand Forks and raged unchecked for several hours.
The president's request for the extra $200 million in aid brings the total amount of assistance that he has sought for the battered states of North Dakota, South Dakota and Minnesota to $488 million.
"Welcome to Grand Forks, Mr. President. Welcome to our nightmare," the Grand Forks Herald said in an editorial in Tuesday's edition in advance of Clinton's arrival.
Roughly 90 percent of this evacuated city of 50,000 was under water from the Red River, which extended its widening path of destruction northward into Canada.

Hundreds of people were evacuated from Drayton, North Dakota, 40 miles (64 km) north of Grand Forks where a cracked dike threatened to give way. Hundreds more left Pembina, and about 750 people across the border in Emerson, Manitoba, fled their homes.
A four-year-old boy living near Portage-la-Prairie, Manitoba, drowned in a culvert along the swollen Assiniboine River, which drains into the Red River.
The catastrophe had cut off all land links between Minnesota and North Dakota along a 150-mile (241 km) stretch from Fargo, North Dakota, to the Canadian border.

The slow-moving Red River reached more than 54 feet (16 metres) at Grand Forks, and could fluctuate at even higher levels on the flat, table-top landscape before receding in a few days. Residents evacuated from both sides of the river, which forms the North Dakota-Minnesota border, were told to be prepared to stay away for two weeks or longer.
Clinton declared the North Dakota-Minnesota-South Dakota region a disaster area two weeks ago in the wake of what experts have called a once-in-500-years flood.

Officials said it was too early to assess the monetary costs of the slow-motion disaster until the waters receded though one unconfirmed local report in Grand Forks said damage could be as high as $1 billion.

Members of Congress representing the flooded states pleaded for massive aid, and White House officials suggested some type of "Marshall Plan" for the region, reminiscent of the programme of aid for Europe after the Second World War.
Upstream at Fargo, the Red River was falling at an increasing rate.
"The river is our friend right now as it continues to drop," said Dennis Walaker, operations manager for Fargo's Public Works department.
